title: Button hierarchy
summary: Learn how primary, secondary, and tertiary buttons tell people what to do next.
objective: Give each view one clear primary action and style the rest by importance.
subject: design

hook.prompt: Which toolbar makes it obvious what to do next?

visual.alt: Three filled buttons in a row: Publish, Preview, and Cancel.

options.feedback: All three shout equally, so nothing stands out.

visual.alt: A filled Publish button, an outlined Preview button, and a text-only Cancel button.

hook.explanation: When one button stands out, people know the main action at a glance.

bricks.title: One primary action per view
bricks.body: The **primary button** is the action you most want people to take. Give each view only one. If everything is primary, nothing is.

visual.alt: Two buttons: a filled Place order and an outlined Back to cart.

bricks.prompt: On a checkout page, which action should be primary?

options.feedback: Useful, but it pulls people away from finishing their purchase.
Only some people need it, so it shouldn't compete with the main action.

bricks.hint: What is the one thing this page exists to help people do?
bricks.explanation: Checkout exists to complete the purchase, so **Place order** is the primary action.

bricks.prompt: This form has two primary buttons. Tap the one that should be demoted.
bricks.explanation: **Learn more** is optional, so it should be secondary or tertiary. **Create account** is the main goal.

bricks.title: Secondary and tertiary buttons
bricks.body: **Secondary** buttons (usually outlined) are for useful alternatives. **Tertiary** buttons (text only) are for low-priority actions like Cancel or Learn more. Less important means less visual weight.

visual.alt: Three buttons side by side: filled Primary, outlined Secondary, and text-only Tertiary.

bricks.prompt: In a document editor, sort each action by how much emphasis it needs.
bricks.explanation: Publishing is the goal. Preview and Save draft are useful alternatives. Cancel and help are rarely needed.

bricks.prompt: Order these buttons from most to least visual weight.
bricks.explanation: A solid fill draws the eye most, an outline less, and plain text least.

bricks.prompt: Which of these dialog footers follow the button hierarchy?

visual.alt: A filled Save button, an outlined Preview button, and a text-only Cancel button.
Two filled buttons side by side: Save and Cancel.

options.feedback: Cancel is filled too, so it competes with Save for attention.

visual.alt: A filled Save button and a text-only Cancel button.
A text-only Save button and a filled Cancel button.

options.feedback: This flips the hierarchy: the main action is the weakest button, and Cancel gets all the weight.

bricks.explanation: A good footer has one filled button for the main action and lighter styles for the rest. That works with two buttons or three.

challenge.prompt: Which plan would you go with?
challenge.situation: A settings page has three actions: **Save changes**, **Reset to defaults**, and **Delete account**.

options.text: Save as primary, Reset as secondary, Delete as a red text button placed apart from the others
options.outcome: The main action is clear, and the dangerous one is hard to hit by accident.

options.text: Save as primary, Reset and Delete as secondary buttons side by side
options.outcome: Clear main action, but Delete sits right next to Reset and looks just as safe.

options.text: All three as primary buttons so they're easy to find
options.outcome: Nothing stands out, and Delete is as tempting as Save.

challenge.hint: Think about both importance and risk.
challenge.explanation: Hierarchy shows importance, and dangerous actions also need distance and a warning color.

takeaways: Give each view one primary action.
Use secondary for useful alternatives and tertiary for low-priority actions.
Keep destructive actions visually distinct and away from the main action.
